opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting tension, and it's one we think about a lot. The way I frame it is that the default posture in AI today is that you hand your data to someone else's server and you trust them. You trust they're not logging it, not training on it, not getting breached. For a lot of what people actually want AI to do, like going through your email, your finances, your health records, and acting on your behalf, that trust model just doesn't hold up.

So the goal with private AI is to flip it. You shouldn't have to trust the operator. You should be able to verify. The practical way to do that today is with secure enclaves, trusted execution environments on modern CPUs and GPUs. The model runs inside the enclave, your data is encrypted going in, and you get a cryptographic attestation that proves what code is running and that nobody, including us or the hardware provider, can see inside.

Now, where the flexibility trade-off comes in: the more freedom you give people to deploy arbitrary models and arbitrary code, the bigger the surface you have to reason about. If anyone can drop in any model with any custom runtime, then attestation tells you that *something* ran, but not necessarily that it's something you'd want to trust. So we try to separate the layers. The infrastructure layer is fixed and verifiable: the enclave, the attestation, how keys are handled, how data flows in and out. On top of that, model developers have a lot of freedom. They can bring open-weight models, fine-tunes, their own agents, and the user can still check exactly which model and which version they're talking to.

There are real costs. Enclaves add some overhead. Not every hardware setup supports confidential computing well yet, especially for large multi-GPU workloads. And the tooling for developers is still maturing. There's also a subtler point: privacy of computation doesn't automatically mean the model is behaving well. A model can run perfectly privately and still be bad at its job or misaligned with what you want. So verifiability of the runtime is necessary, but it's not the whole story. You also want openness around the models themselves, and eventually ways to verify how they were trained.

My general philosophy is that security should be the floor, not a premium feature. You shouldn't have to pick between a capable model and a private one. Flexibility is valuable, but it has to be built on top of guarantees that hold no matter what gets deployed. If we get that right, developers get to innovate freely, and users don't have to take anyone's word for it, because they can check.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing of it as a trade-off is actually where a lot of people go wrong, because the way most of the industry approaches it is, you pick a model, you pick a cloud, and then you kind of bolt security on afterward. And then of course it feels like a trade-off, because every time you want to swap a model or move to a different provider you're re-doing all of the trust assumptions.

The way we think about it at NEAR AI is, the user is the one who should own the security guarantees, not the model provider and not the operator. So the whole stack is built around confidential computing. The model runs inside a TEE, the inputs and outputs are encrypted end to end, and the user, or the agent acting on behalf of the user, can actually verify through attestation what code and what model weights are running before it ever sends a token of data. That's the security layer.

And once you have that, the flexibility becomes almost free, because the security guarantee is not tied to a specific model. You can run an open-source Llama, you can run DeepSeek, you can run something somebody fine-tuned yesterday, and from the user's perspective the question is the same: can I verify what's running in that enclave, and do I trust that configuration? The model becomes a swappable component behind a trust boundary that doesn't move.

Now, there are real constraints, I don't want to pretend there aren't. Confidential computing hardware has historically had limitations on what you can run inside of it, especially on GPUs, and there's a performance overhead. So a year or two ago, if you wanted a 400B parameter model inside a TEE, that was genuinely hard. That's gotten dramatically better with the newer NVIDIA hardware, and we spend a lot of effort on the inference side making that overhead small enough that developers don't really feel it.

The other place where there's a real tension is closed models. If someone wants to run a frontier model from one of the big labs, those weights are not going to be shipped into an enclave you control. So there you do make a choice: you either accept that you're trusting that provider with your data, or you use an open model where you get the full verifiable guarantee. Our bet is that the gap between open and closed models is closing fast enough that for most actual use cases, the open model inside a verifiable environment is the better deal, because you get something you can't get from a closed API, which is proof.

And I think that matters a lot more as we move toward agents. When it's a chatbot, okay, maybe you're fine with the privacy policy. When it's an agent that has your keys, your email, your financial data, and is taking actions on your behalf, "trust us" isn't a good enough answer. You want cryptographic certainty about what's touching that data. So from my point of view, security isn't the thing you give up to get flexibility. Done right, it's the thing that lets you be flexible, because you can swap anything underneath and the user never has to re-trust you.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to give people flexibility in what model they run without making the privacy guarantees depend on which model they choose. You should be able to bring a model that fits your use case, but that model shouldn’t automatically get access to all of your data or permission to send it somewhere.

So you separate the model from the security boundary. What information can it access? What tools can it call? Can it communicate outside the private environment? Those permissions need to be enforced by the environment, rather than by asking the model to behave.

There is a trade-off when you start connecting external services, because now you’re extending that trust boundary. I’d make those connections explicit and narrowly scoped. The default should protect the user’s data, and the user should understand when an action changes that guarantee.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to separate flexibility in choosing a model from permission to access your data. You should be able to bring different models into your private environment, but that shouldn’t automatically give the model—or whoever operates it—access to everything you have.

The trade-off becomes much harder if switching models means sending your information to a different provider. Ideally, you bring the computation to the data, keep access scoped to the task, and make it clear to the user when information is leaving that boundary. So you can have flexibility, but security has to be a property of the environment, rather than something you hope each model provider will handle.
